## Inductive bias in visual learning

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm]
\node[text=conv,font=\bfseries] at (2,3.5) {Convolution};
\node[text=attn,font=\bfseries] at (10,3.5) {Attention};
\foreach \offset in {0,8} {
  \foreach \x in {0,...,4} {\foreach \y in {0,...,3} {
    \draw[border,fill=surface] (\offset+\x*.7,\y*.7) rectangle +(0.6,0.6);
  }}
}
\foreach \x in {1,...,3} {\foreach \y in {0,...,2} {
  \draw[conv,fill=conv!20!canvas] (\x*.7,\y*.7) rectangle +(0.6,0.6);
}}
\fill[conv] (1.4,.7) rectangle +(0.6,0.6);
\foreach \x/\y in {0/3,1/0,4/2,4/0} {
 \draw[attn,fill=attn!20!canvas] (8+\x*.7,\y*.7) rectangle +(0.6,0.6);
 \draw[attn,line width=.8pt] (9.7,1) -- (8+\x*.7+.3,\y*.7+.3);
}
\fill[attn] (9.4,.7) rectangle +(.6,.6);
\node[align=center,text width=5.2cm] at (1.7,-.65) {Reuse a local filter\\across the image};
\node[align=center,text width=5.2cm] at (9.7,-.65) {Choose connections\\from the input};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

```{=latex}
Convolution builds in local structure;\\
attention leaves more spatial relationships to be learned.
```

::: notes
Source and context: Dai et al. (2021), §§1–2.1 and Table 1. The schematic feature maps are reused from the original deck, not measured attention. Full attention can use every location.

Timing: 1:00. Title introduction: 0:20. Introduce the NeurIPS 2021 paper by Dai, Liu, Le, and Tan, then ask: how can useful assumptions and flexible learning work together?

Start with the visual: each square is a feature-map location and the solid square is the location being updated. The blue neighborhood illustrates a shared local filter. The purple connections illustrate input-dependent mixing across the map; only a few links are drawn for clarity, while CoAtNet uses global attention. Convolution can also build a large receptive field through depth. Then define inductive bias: an assumption built into a learning system that favors some solutions over others. Here bias means a learning preference, not social bias. Convolution builds in locality and weight sharing. Its filters are learned, not hand-coded; sharing them is the architectural assumption. This helps reuse a pattern at different locations. Attention computes input-dependent mixing weights using learned projections and can connect distant features. Attention also has inductive biases; avoid saying it has none. The paper argues for a particular balance in its 2021 experiments, not a universal law about every CNN or Transformer.

The paper's hypothesis is that spatial structure helps generalization while attention's flexibility helps fit large datasets. Generalization means doing well on unseen examples. Capacity here means the ability to fit a large training dataset under the tested training budget, not parameter count. Explain these terms in plain language now so the later evidence is easy to follow. Use the bottom caption to connect the visual to the next slide: convolution builds in locality and shared filtering, while global attention leaves more spatial relationships to be learned from data. This does not mean attention is free of inductive bias. Transition: if local patterns matter especially early, convolution is a sensible starting point, with attention connecting the resulting features later.
:::

## Why convolution before attention?

**The prior:** local patterns favor convolution early.

```{=latex}
\vspace{.7em}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm]
\node[text=conv,font=\bfseries] at (1.6,1.7) {Convolution};
\node[text=muted,font=\bfseries] at (6.1,1.7) {Downsampling};
\node[text=attn,font=\bfseries] at (10.6,1.7) {Attention};
\node[align=center,text width=3.3cm,font=\large] at (1.6,.65) {Local\\features};
\node[align=center,text width=3.3cm,font=\large] at (6.1,.65) {Fewer\\locations};
\node[align=center,text width=3.3cm,font=\large] at (10.6,.65) {Global\\relationships};
\draw[flow] (3.35,.65)--(4.3,.65);
\draw[flow] (7.85,.65)--(8.8,.65);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\vspace{.8em}
\textbf{Downsampling makes global attention cheaper.}
```

::: notes
Source and context: Dai et al. (2021), §2.2. Global attention has quadratic cost in the number of spatial locations.

Timing: 0:55. Follow the visual from local features through fewer locations to global relationships. The three labels describe a processing rationale, not three literal network stages: downsampling happens throughout the multistage network. Separate the two reasons for the order. First is the inductive-bias argument: local patterns are expected to be more common in early processing, so convolution is a sensible starting point. Second is cost: global attention compares every pair of spatial locations. Reducing the feature-map size makes that operation practical. Convolution is not the only way to downsample; the paper also tests a ViT-style stem.

The authors explicitly constrain the multistage layouts to put convolution before Transformer stages. This is a choice guided by their prior, not a conclusion from testing all permutations. The early MBConv stage is fixed because the spatial size is too large for their global attention. Avoid claiming that attention-first networks are impossible, or that early convolutions cannot eventually gather global context. Transition: here is exactly what that restricted experiment compares.
:::

## What the authors actually compared

```{=latex}
\begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
\begin{column}{.43\textwidth}
\textbf{Four stage layouts}

\vspace{.7em}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm]
\foreach \row in {0,...,3} {
 \foreach \j in {1,...,4} {
  \pgfmathtruncatemacro{\isT}{\j>4-\row}
  \ifnum\isT=1\def\col{attn}\def\letter{T}\else\def\col{conv}\def\letter{C}\fi
  \node[draw=\col,fill=\col!14!canvas,minimum width=.82cm,minimum height=.58cm,text=\col] at (\j*1.05,-\row*.79) {\letter};
 }
}
\draw[good,line width=.8pt] (.53,-1.98) rectangle (4.72,-1.18);
\node[anchor=west,text=good,font=\footnotesize] at (4.85,-1.58) {Selected};
\end{tikzpicture}

{\small C = convolution\\T = relative attention}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{.53\textwidth}
\textbf{Plus a ViT-style comparator}

\vspace{.7em}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm]
\node[draw=muted,fill=surface,minimum width=1.25cm,minimum height=.85cm,align=center,font=\footnotesize] at (.65,0) {Patch\\stem};
\draw[flow] (1.4,0)--(1.9,0);
\node[draw=attn,fill=attn!14!canvas,minimum width=3.2cm,minimum height=.85cm,text=attn,align=center,font=\footnotesize] at (3.6,0) {Relative-attention\\stack};
\end{tikzpicture}

\vspace{.9em}
\textcolor{warm}{\textbf{Outside this search}}\\
Alternating stages\\
Attention $\rightarrow$ convolution
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\vspace{1em}
Similar model sizes and compute; ImageNet-1K and JFT.
```

::: notes
Source and context: Dai et al. (2021), §2.2, Figure 1 and Table 2. Layout study: no augmentation or regularization; not an exhaustive architecture search.

Timing: 1:05. Walk through the four rows as progressively earlier switches to attention. C-C-C-C never switches. C-C-C-T switches only at the last stage. C-C-T-T switches halfway through the four named stages. C-T-T-T retains one MBConv stage after the common convolutional stem. Each letter on the left represents a stage containing multiple blocks; the common convolutional stem is omitted. The single stack box on the right represents the ViT-style comparator's relative-attention blocks, not one layer or a specified number of stages. The green outline identifies C-C-T-T as the selected multistage layout. All T operations shown use relative attention.

The fifth comparator uses a ViT-style patch stem and relative-attention blocks. It is important to include it: the authors did compare an attention-dominated model, but did not test a multistage attention-then-convolution ordering. Alternation and reversed orders are outside the reported study, so their absence is not evidence that they are worse. The provided paper lacks the appendices it references; limit the statement to the reported layout study in §2.2.

The five variants have comparable parameter counts and compute. They are trained on ImageNet-1K for 300 epochs and JFT for three epochs without augmentation or regularization. ImageNet-1K has about 1.28 million training images; this JFT experiment uses over 300 million. This experiment isolates layout more directly than the later cross-model benchmarks.

Brief spoken evidence: “C-C-T-T retained strong large-data fitting while transferring better than C-T-T-T. That supported the authors' choice of this balance.” Both fit JFT similarly, with pretraining precision of 34.40 versus 34.36. After adaptation to ImageNet, C-C-T-T reached 82.39% accuracy versus 81.78% for C-T-T-T, a 0.61-percentage-point gain at 224×224 evaluation. Transfer means adapting the pretrained model to ImageNet; top-1 accuracy means the first-choice class is correct. Transition: here is how that selected layout becomes the full network.
:::

## Selected layout: C-C-T-T

```{=latex}

\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm]
\foreach \x/\w/\h/\col/\stage/\kind/\res in {
0/1.8/2.4/conv/S0/{}/2,

}
\node[text=conv,font=\bfseries,align=center] at (.9,1.2) {Conv\\stem};
\node[text=muted,font=\footnotesize] at (7.4,2.75) {Lower spatial resolution $\longrightarrow$};
\foreach \x/\y/\letter/\col in {3.6/1/C/conv,6.2/.8/C/conv,8.8/.6/T/attn,11.4/.4/T/attn} {
 \node[text=\col,font=\large\bfseries] at (\x,\y) {\letter};
}
\foreach \a/\b in {1.9/2.7,4.5/5.4,7/8.1,9.5/10.8} {\draw[flow] (\a,.6) -- (\b,.6);}
\node[anchor=west,text=conv] at (0,-1.65) {Learn local patterns};

```

```{=latex}
\textbf{Inside attention:} content match + relative-position bias.
```


::: notes
Source and context: C-C-T-T names S1–S4; convolution stages use MBConv. Schematic sizes. Dai et al. (2021), §§2.1–2.2 and Tables 3 and 6.

Timing: 0:55. Read the diagram from left to right: convolutional stem, two MBConv stages, then two relative-attention stages. S0 is a two-layer convolutional stem that turns image pixels into initial feature maps at half the input height and width. The C, C, T, T labels name S1 through S4 and connect directly to the selected row on the preceding slide; the common stem is separate from those four letters. The boxes represent shrinking spatial maps, not parameter counts. Channels increase as spatial size decreases, and each stage contains multiple blocks.

This brings the two design choices together: early convolution supplies local processing, while late attention retains a spatial prior through its learned relative-position bias. Explain the compact caption: attention combines a content match with a learned preference for relative displacement. That preference is shared across pairs with the same offset and can depend on direction as well as distance; it need not always favor nearby features. Smaller feature maps reduce the cost of comparing all pairs of locations. With N locations, the attention matrix has N squared entries; halving both image dimensions cuts that matrix cost by about sixteen, not the runtime of the whole network. Brief spoken evidence: “Keeping the relative-position bias also helped: 85.7% accuracy versus 85.3% without it.” This is a separate ImageNet-only experiment at 384×384, a gain of 0.4 percentage points. Do not add this gain to the layout comparison on slide 4; neither comparison reports repeated-seed uncertainty. Transition: with the architecture in place, how does CoAtNet compare as models get larger?
:::

Source and context: Figure 2 in this deck is redrawn from Dai et al. (2021), Tables 4–5. Fourteen selected reported results from five model families. Only the supplied thirteen-page paper was reviewed; its referenced appendices are absent.

::: notes
Source and context: Interpretation of the preceding two charts, based on Dai et al. (2021), Figure 3 and Tables 4–5. These are historical benchmark comparisons, distinct from the controlled design-choice experiments discussed in the notes for slides 4 and 5.

Timing: 0:50. Connect the results to the opening convolution-versus-attention story using two separate comparisons. CoAtNet-3 is compared with convolution-only NFNet-F5 on the left; CoAtNet-4 is compared with attention-based ViT-H/14 on the right. These are different CoAtNet variants and training settings, not a single three-model controlled experiment. All accuracies are final ImageNet top-1. Model size means parameter count, not measured runtime or training cost.

Start with the convolution-only comparison: CoAtNet-3 and NFNet-F5 both reach 86.0% accuracy with ImageNet-1K training only, using 168M and 377M parameters respectively (Table 4). The ratio 377/168 is approximately 2.24, summarized as 2.2 times fewer parameters. Both use 1.28M training images without external pretraining, but evaluation sizes differ: 512×512 for CoAtNet-3 and 544×544 for NFNet-F5. This is matched reported accuracy, not evidence of statistical equivalence.

Then explain the attention-based comparison: CoAtNet-4 reaches 88.56% ImageNet accuracy with 275M parameters and ImageNet-21K pretraining (12.7M images), while ViT-H/14 reaches 88.55% with 632M parameters and JFT-300M pretraining. Their accuracies are effectively matched at about 88.6%; this is not a claim of statistically significant superiority. The parameter ratio is 632/275, approximately 2.3. The image-count ratio is 300/12.7, approximately 23.6; the slide follows the paper's approximate 23-times characterization. Equivalently, CoAtNet uses about 44% as many parameters and about 4% as many pretraining images. The CoAtNet-4 result uses PT-RA-E150 and 512×512 evaluation; ViT-H/14 uses 518×518 evaluation. These reported systems differ in dataset and training recipe, so this is not a controlled estimate of data efficiency.

Optional supporting comparison for questions: at 3B images, CoAtNet-7 reaches 90.88% compared with ViT-G/14's 90.45%.

Brief spoken interpretation: “The results support combining convolution's spatial biases with attention's flexible global interactions.” Relate this to the architecture: early convolution supplies useful local processing, while later attention connects features globally; relative-position bias retains spatial structure within attention. This balance performs well in the tested image-classification settings. These charts do not isolate the causal effect of architecture or training-data quantity. Model sizes and variants, dataset content, training recipes, compute, and evaluation resolutions vary; external baselines were not all retrained under one shared protocol. Do not claim universal superiority or statistical significance. The separate stage-layout and position-bias checks are the more direct evidence about those design choices, and their numerical findings remain in slides 4–5's notes.

Transition: these results are promising, but two gaps remain: alternative stage orders and truly small datasets.
:::

Source and context: Evidence boundaries from Dai et al. (2021), §§2.2 and 4. The next test is a proposed follow-up, not a reported experiment.

Timing: 0:55. Bring back the early caveat now that the audience understands the results. The blue C and purple T boxes reuse the stage notation from slides 4 and 5. C-T-C-T and T-T-C-C are illustrative untested multistage orders, not models measured in the paper; the common stem is omitted. The authors' local-first prior narrows the architecture search, so the evidence does not establish that alternating or reversed layouts are inferior. C-C-T-T is supported within the chosen search space. The ViT-style stem comparator was included; do not imply that all attention-dominated designs were excluded. State the limit as applying to the reported layout experiment.

The second boundary is data size. ImageNet-1K is small relative to hundreds of millions or billions, but is not small in the everyday sense of a few hundred or thousand examples. Lack of a test is not a reported failure. A follow-up could compare stage orders with similar parameter counts, compute, pretraining, augmentation, training budget, and multiple seeds on small training subsets. Matching pretraining is essential: otherwise a small fine-tuning set still benefits from a large earlier dataset. Do not introduce audio-project results as evidence for this paper.

Transition: these limits narrow the claim while leaving a clear design lesson.
:::
